notes: Scatter rock: pebbles, slabs, boulders and outcrop courses — the form ART_BIBLE 1 calls the most characteristic thing in the reference. GRADE MEASURED, NOT AUTHORED FROM MEMORY. Sampled off refs/genshin/grasslands.jpg: lit rock facet #BBD9BE (H126 S0.139 luma 0.818), a partly-turned facet #ACCAB3 (luma 0.762), the DARKEST rock facet in the frame #397097 (luma 0.404), and intra-facet luma sd 0.0155-0.0371 over a 20x20 window. The value range across rock facets is p02 0.444 / p50 0.635 / p90 0.791 — a tight high-key band, shadow-to-lit ratio about 0.49, NOT a bright top over a navy side. The albedo stops therefore sit in one narrow luma band and differ mainly in HUE — shadow cooler and bluer, lit rotated toward yellow-green and LESS saturated per ART_BIBLE 2 — while `ambient` carries the value. In this material the shadow stop is albedo x ambient and nothing else, so a shadow stop that is dark in the ALBEDO is a hole in the picture no matter what hue it is. WHY THIS DEF EXISTS RATHER THAN AN EDIT TO `rock`/`mountain`/`foliage`/`bush`. src/world/surfaceGrade.ts applies `graded(surfaceId, params)` at the point of use, and `graded` is `{...params, ...CLEAN, ...GRADE[surfaceId]}` — so for the four ids it has an entry for, the GRADE table wins over BOTH the def and the per-def `material` override. Authoring a corrected value on `rock` therefore changed the Forge and left the game pixel exactly where it was, which is how the last round shipped a rock whose authored shadow (luma 0.51) arrived on screen at #232E66 (luma 0.187) against the reference's darkest rock facet at 0.404. These are the scatter library's OWN surface ids, so only `CLEAN` applies to them — which is what we want anyway — and the measured grade below reaches the pixel in both the Forge and the game. The old ids stay for the terrain, which is the world team's to grade. `topGain` and `gradientStrength` carry the INTRA-FACET variation. With the brush overlay gone a plane-cut facet measured luma sd 0.000-0.005 over a 60x60 window against 0.0155-0.0371 for a rock facet in the reference — flatter than the target by an order of magnitude, which reads as plastic and trips a dead-flat-tile check. The variation the reference has is a smooth vertical ramp following the FORM (ART_BIBLE 3: the vertical gradient 'is doing enormous work'), not noise, so it comes from the up-axis sweep rather than from a stroke field. `shadowSkyTint` pulled back to ~0.1. This is what was actually making the rock a NAVY CUBE, not the authored hex: the param replaces the shadow albedo with the live sky HUE at the shadow's own luminance and then runs it through `boostSaturation`, so an authored blue-grey at S0.16 arrived on screen at S0.64 hue 222 and lost most of its value doing it — measured #2B4278 luma 0.255 at noon from an authored #82919B at luma 0.58. ART_BIBLE 2 wants the shade COOLED, not recoloured, and the reference's own darkest rock facet is #397097 at luma 0.404. A small tint plus a high ambient gets both; a large tint gets neither. AMBIENT AND ALBEDO SOLVED TOGETHER, from the render rather than by eye. In this material the shadow stop is albedo x ambient and nothing else (`color = albedo * (ambient + direct)` in painterly.ts), so a facet turned away from the sun can only be lifted by the albedo or by the ambient scale. Fitted from two measured samples on a rock-medium close-up at noon (shaded facet #2C4374 -> 0.0546 linear, lit facet #91B3B0 -> 0.4106 linear) the ambient term was 0.19 and the direct term 1.10 in linear units; solving for a shaded facet at the reference's 0.404 and a lit facet at its p90 of 0.79 puts the ambient scale at 4.2 with both albedo stops in ONE narrow linear-luma band around 0.36. That is why the three stops look almost the same value here and differ mainly in hue: the reference's rock does the same thing — shadow-to-lit ratio 0.49 with every facet inside p02 0.444 .. p90 0.791.
